chapters.title: Breakouts, pullbacks & failed moves
chapters.subtitle: Define the boundary and the observation time before evaluating a crossing.
chapters.takeaway: A breakout is a predefined crossing, not a promise. Confirmation and retests trade additional information for changed timing and execution.

sections.title: A crossing needs a boundary and a clock
paragraphs: A breakout is a move beyond a previously identified price boundary or area. The word by itself is incomplete: beyond which edge, by how much, using what price field, and at what observation time? An intraday high above resistance and a completed close above it are different conditions. Both are legitimate observations, but they define different events. A downward crossing is often called a breakdown.

Imagine Harbor has a resistance area from $49.70 to $50.00. A trade at $50.01 crosses the upper edge, yet a rule requiring a close more than 1% above that edge needs a close above $50.50. The small buffer is an illustrative convention, not an optimized or universally effective threshold. Fix it beforehand. A level selected after seeing the crossing cannot fairly demonstrate that you recognized a breakout in advance.

sections.title: The exact price field changes the result
paragraphs: Suppose a fictional daily bar opens at $49.40, reaches $50.80, falls to $49.10, and closes at $49.70. It crossed $50 intraday but did not finish above it. An intraday-break rule triggered; a close-above-$50 rule did not; a close-above-$50.50 rule also did not. Describing the move as false without naming the rule hides these differences. The label should refer to the event you actually defined.

If you require the completed close, that information becomes available at the end of the session. A backtest must then use a feasible subsequent execution convention, or an explicitly justified closing-auction model with its actual order and information deadlines. It cannot simply observe the finalized closing signal and assume a guaranteed trade at the same price. The decision clock is part of the method. Treating timing as an afterthought can make a historical breakout system appear better than it could have been.

sections.title: Confirmation filters add requirements, not certainty
paragraphs: Some rules require a buffer, repeated closes, increased volume, or several conditions together. These filters select a different set of observations and often delay recognition. They may remove some failed moves and exclude some successful ones. Whether the tradeoff is useful depends on measurement across the relevant universe and period. Calling a condition confirmation does not confer statistical independence or proven effectiveness.

Consider an illustrative close above $50 with volume at least 1.5 times the prior twenty-session mean. A $50.80 close on 1.6 times volume satisfies it. A $52 close on 1.2 times volume does not, even if price keeps rising later. That exclusion is part of the rule rather than an error to correct with hindsight. If you relax the volume requirement only on the examples that subsequently succeed, you are changing the method after learning the outcome.

sections.title: Retests are optional paths
paragraphs: After an upward crossing, price may revisit the former boundary; after a downward crossing, it may revisit from below. Retest, pullback, and throwback terminology varies, so this book describes the direction explicitly. A return toward the area is an observation. A supportive reaction or renewed decline requires another defined condition. Price may also continue without returning at all.

If Harbor closes at $51 beyond a $50 boundary, a retest rule might require a later low inside $49.80–$50.20 followed by a close above $50.50 within three sessions. This original convention makes the hypothesis testable. A low of $50.30 misses the specified visit, and a low of $49 followed by a $49.50 close does not meet the supportive-close condition. Waiting can improve the prospective entry price in some paths, miss others, or encounter an actual failure. Record all three possibilities.

sections.title: Execution can change the economics
paragraphs: Suppose the illustrative signal close is $50.80, a planned protective trigger is $48.80, and a geometric reference is $54.80. At the signal price, nominal downside distance is $2 and upside distance is $4. The next open is $52.20. Entering then changes those distances to $3.40 and $2.60, respectively. Their ratio changes from 2.0 to about 0.76. Neither calculation is an expectancy because it supplies no probabilities or execution guarantees.

An overnight gap can also pass an intended order level entirely. A market order seeks execution but does not guarantee the displayed price; a limit sets a price constraint but may not fill; a stop-market order activates a market order when its trigger is reached. These distinctions matter when a chart makes an entry look exact. A valid signal can lead to a poor executable opportunity under the chosen plan, and declining that opportunity is consistent with having recognized the chart event accurately.

sections.title: Define failure without selecting the answer
paragraphs: A false-break definition needs a time window and a return condition. One illustrative rule calls an upward closing breakout failed if any of the next three completed closes is below the original $50 boundary. Another requires price to hit a protective trigger. They are different outcome measures. Neither can label the event failed at the instant of the initial crossing; the later observations have not happened yet.

A failed upward move does not automatically prove a profitable short trade. Reversing direction introduces a new entry, costs, risk, and a hypothesis that can fail independently. Price may oscillate across the area repeatedly. Study the full sequence instead of drawing arrows only on the profitable sections. Breakout analysis becomes useful when it forces you to specify boundaries, timing, execution, and update rules. Its value should be evaluated through that complete process, not through a collection of memorable escape-from-the-range pictures.

sections.title: Freeze a small plan before revealing the continuation
paragraphs: Return to the main Harbor chart. Its session-9 close is $50.80 and session-10 close is $49.40. Before session 9, the resistance area is already fixed at $49.70–$50.00. For this exercise, use a completed regular-session close strictly above $50.50 as the signal. Volume is not an additional condition in this main rule; the earlier volume-filter example is a separate comparison. Declare failure if any of the next three completed closes is strictly below $50.00. Equality at either threshold does not qualify. These arbitrary rules are supplied so two readers can classify the same sequence without supplying missing decisions.

Freeze the following paper execution model after the session-9 close. Use only the next session’s opening observation. If that open is above $50.80, skip the candidate entirely, even if price later returns. Otherwise model 50 shares filled at the open, provided it is above the $48.80 protective trigger. An open at or below the protective trigger is also a skip. Model a sell stop at $48.80 and a sell limit target at $54.80; if neither exits the position by the third post-signal session, model an exit at that session’s close. A later opening gap through the stop uses the opening price, not $48.80. If an ordinary OHLC bar spans both exits without an opening gap deciding the first event, mark the result sequence-ambiguous rather than inventing an order. All fills here are explicit teaching assumptions, not deductions from a real order book.

At the maximum allowed entry of $50.80, 50 shares have $2,540 entry notional before costs and $100 planned price risk: 50 × ($50.80 − $48.80). This paper plan assumes sufficient cash, one position, no borrowing, and a fixed $5 round-trip expense, charged $2.50 on entry and $2.50 on exit. Reserve $2,542.50 before entry to cover the maximum entry debit. Freeze 1R after the modeled fill as 50 × (entry price − $48.80); an eligible lower entry has a smaller price-risk denominator. At $50.80, the ordinary cost-inclusive modeled loss is $105, or −1.05R net, and the exact target exit is +$195, or +1.95R net. Costs are separate from the price-risk denominator; a $100 all-in loss budget would require a smaller quantity at this entry. A gap can exceed either budget.

Now reveal the main continuation: session 10 opens at $52.20, reaches $52.60, falls to $49.10, and closes at $49.40. At the open the plan records a skip; at the close the chart event meets the failure definition. No trade occurred, so the journal records no realized trade P&L or R outcome. The hypothetical distances from a chased $52.20 entry remain useful for comparison, but do not become this plan’s account result. Observation, eligibility, and outcome each have their own timestamp.

sections.title: Read a retest with the future covered
paragraphs: Use a separate retest example to practice chronological interpretation. At the signal close of $51, the fixed boundary is $50 and the visit area is $49.80–$50.20. Require a later low inside that area and a close above $50.50 in the same session, within three sessions after the signal. On the first later session, L50.30/C50.80 fails the visit condition. On the second, L50.10/C50.60 meets both conditions; the event becomes known only at that second close. A third session cannot be used to recognize it earlier.

Contrast two branches at that same second-session cutoff. L50.10/C50.40 visits but fails the closing condition. L49.00/C50.60 fails this specific low-inside-area rule because the measured low is outside it. The low and close do not prove that a trade occurred inside the area: eligible transaction prices can jump over intervening values. A different rule based on any traded touch needs the relevant transaction record or an explicit inference convention. State the field you measured. These alternatives show why a rule must be read literally before its usefulness is judged.

For a concrete counterexample, take two complete fictional eligible-price tapes. Tape A is 49.30 → 49.00 → 50.60. Tape B is 49.30 → 49.00 → 50.00 → 50.60. Both have O49.30/H50.60/L49.00/C50.60; both fail the low-inside-$49.80–$50.20 rule. Only B contains a traded touch at $50.00. A line drawn between A’s $49.00 and $50.60 marks passes across the area on paper, but that connecting stroke does not supply a transaction. Without the tapes, their identical OHLC cannot distinguish the touch outcomes.

example.title: A correct signal can end in a skip
example.text: At the session-9 close, $50.80 exceeds the frozen $50.50 threshold. At the session-10 open, $52.20 exceeds the entry ceiling, so the paper plan skips. At the session-10 close, $49.40 is below the $50 boundary and meets the failure definition. The three statements are compatible. No position was opened, so neither a hypothetical stop loss nor the foregone target belongs in realized P&L.

outcomes: Determine when a fixed closing-breakout rule becomes observable.
Separate signal recognition, an eligible entry, and a later failure.
Reproduce the quantity, costs, and R result (profit or loss as a multiple of planned price risk) of a fully stated paper plan.
Retain successful, failed, skipped, and ambiguous continuations in a review.
solution: At the session-9 close, 50.80 > 50.50 establishes a signal; the next open and later failure are still unknown. At the session-10 open, 52.20 > 50.80 requires a skip. At its close, 49.40 < 50.00 establishes failure inside the three-session window. There is no trade P&L, because there was no entry; a skip is a retained opportunity record rather than a zero-R executed trade.

For the explicitly modeled $50.80 target branch: entry notional = 50 × $50.80 = $2,540; entry cash debit = $2,542.50 including the $2.50 entry charge. Planned price risk = 50 × $2 = $100; ordinary loss including $5 expense = $105. Target price profit = 50 × $4 = $200; net profit = $195; net R = 195/100 = +1.95R. The denominator is frozen filled-price risk, not notional or the $105 cost-inclusive loss.

The comparison branches are invented continuations for inspecting the same plan. Their count is not a sample of strategy success rates. A bar containing both exit prices would require the declared ambiguity policy.

practice.title: Follow the retest clock
practice.question: Using the retest rule, classify day +1 L50.30/C50.80 and day +2 L50.10/C50.60. What changes if day +2 closes at $50.40?
solution: Day +1 misses the low-inside-$49.80–$50.20 condition. Day +2 meets the visit and close-above-$50.50 conditions, recognized at its close. With C50.40, the visit occurs but the closing condition fails; neither version licenses a day +1 recognition.

practice.title: A gap changes the realized loss
practice.question: A comparison branch first models 50 shares bought at $50.80. The following session opens at $47.80, below the $48.80 stop. Under the supplied gap rule and $5 expense, calculate the exit, net P&L, and R. Explain why the ordinary $105 modeled loss is not the answer.
solution: The gap rule exits at the assumed $47.80 open. Price loss = 50 × ($50.80 − $47.80) = $150; net P&L = −$155; R = −155/100 = −1.55R. The trigger was skipped by the gap, so an exact $48.80 fill cannot be assumed. The $105 figure described an ordinary exact-trigger exit, not a maximum possible loss.

practice.title: Keep R tied to the eligible fill
practice.question: A separate permitted branch opens at $50.40 and models the same 50-share entry, $48.80 stop, $54.80 target and $5 round-trip charge. Calculate frozen 1R, entry cash debit, net target result and net ordinary-stop result in dollars and R. How much of the maximum-entry cash reserve is released?
solution: The $50.40 opening entry is above $48.80 and at or below $50.80, so it is eligible. Frozen 1R = 50 × ($50.40 − $48.80) = $80. Entry notional is $2,520; cash debit is $2,522.50. The $2,542.50 maximum-entry reserve releases $20.

Target gross profit = 50 × $4.40 = $220; net = $215; net R = 215/80 = +2.6875R. Ordinary-stop net loss = −$80 − $5 = −$85, or −1.0625R. Reusing the maximum-entry $100 denominator would conceal the smaller filled-price risk.

practice.title: A traded touch needs a traded price
practice.question: A different retest area is $72.80–$73.20 inclusive. For each complete fictional eligible-price tape below, reconstruct OHLC and apply two rules: the completed low must be inside the area; or at least one eligible trade must be inside it. Both rules additionally require a close strictly above $73.50. Explain what an OHLC-only observer cannot distinguish.

tables.title: Complete unfamiliar eligible-price tapes (fictional USD)
columns: All eligible trade prices, in order ($)

solution: Both summarize as O72.30/H73.60/L72.00/C73.60. The low is below the area, so neither passes the low-inside-area rule; both satisfy the separate close-above-$73.50 condition.

C has no eligible trade in $72.80–$73.20, while D contains $73.00, so only D passes the traded-touch rule. The jump from $72.00 to $73.60 does not establish intermediate transactions. With only the identical OHLC, traded touch is unresolved; it cannot be inferred by drawing a continuous line.

learnerAttempt.title: First pass: write the Harbor instruction at the session-9 close
paragraphs: The first two sections distinguish price fields and observation times. Pause the main fictional Harbor case at the completed session-9 close. The resistance area $49.70–$50.00 and rules below were supplied before this cutoff; they are not selected from the future path. All nine closes and the complete session-9 candle are shown. The next session has not opened.

Apply the closing signal rule. Record what is observable now and what cannot yet be recorded about entry eligibility, a filled position or a later failure. Write the exact next-opening gate, including equality at both edges, the deadline and the behavior after a rejected open.

This book reports trade results in R. 1R is the price risk planned on the filled position: shares × (entry − initial stop), the loss if the stop fills exactly, before fees. Net R = net P&L ÷ 1R, so −2R means losing twice what the plan risked, and trades of different sizes can be compared. Calculate the maximum-entry cash reservation including the entry fee, the maximum allowed entry’s price-risk 1R and its ordinary cost-inclusive stop loss. Give the formula that freezes 1R if the eligible opening entry is lower. State which later bar fields and modeled execution assumptions would be needed to calculate a realized result.

Save the cutoff note before revealing the full Harbor path and the separate comparison branches. The volume-filter and retest examples later in the chapter are different rules; neither is an extra gate for this main plan. The constructed paths teach accounting and chronology, not return probabilities or a recommended allocation.

foundations.title: Turn a chart into a reproducible observation

tasks.title: Read an unfamiliar candle
tasks.question: A regular-session daily candle has O80/H86/L78/C84. The previous close was $88. Calculate body, upper shadow, lower shadow, total range, open-to-close return, and close-to-close return. Give two ordered routes consistent with it.
solution: Body = $4; upper shadow = $2; lower shadow = $2; range = $8. Open-to-close return = 4/80 = +5%. Close-to-close return = −4/88 = −4.5455%. The rising body does not imply a positive return from the previous close.
80 → 86 → 78 → 84 and 80 → 78 → 86 → 84 both match OHLC. Their order differs; a first-hit exit outcome cannot be recovered from those four prices alone.

tasks.title: Align the comparison
tasks.question: A completed session has volume 1.2 million shares; its five prior completed-session volumes are 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 0.9, and 1.1 million. A new session has 0.6 million by noon, compared with 0.4 million on average at the same cutoff. Calculate both meaningful relative-volume ratios. Can noon volume be ranked against completed-day volume on the same basis?
solution: Prior full-day mean = 5.0/5 = 1.0 million; completed-session ratio = 1.2/1.0 = 1.2. Matched-noon ratio = 0.6/0.4 = 1.5. Dividing noon volume by a completed-day baseline describes a partial/full comparison, not the same activity measure.
Record session boundaries, adjustment conventions, cutoff, and baseline before interpreting either ratio. A future final daily volume is unavailable at noon.

tasks.title: Check the unit before describing a fall
tasks.question: A hypothetical two-for-one split turns 20 shares quoted at $80 into 40 shares quoted at $40 before other movement. An unadjusted chart displays an apparent 50% fall. Write an observation, a data check, and an interpretation to withhold.
solution: Value is 20 × $80 = 40 × $40 = $1,600. The share-price unit changed; the split alone did not produce a 50% ownership-value loss.

Request consistent split-adjusted prior prices and a declared volume convention. Withhold a support-break interpretation until comparable units are confirmed; the algebra is not a forecast of subsequent prices.

price-action.title: Write an analysis with the next bars covered

tasks.title: Freeze the map
tasks.question: Prior recognized reaction highs are $59.70 and $60.00; the chosen resistance area is $59.70–$60.00. At cutoff T, a completed close is $60.50. A predeclared signal requires a close strictly above $60.60. Record observation, rule result, alternative interpretation, and what remains unknown.
solution: Observation: C60.50 is above the area’s upper edge by $0.50. Rule result: no signal, because 60.50 is not strictly above 60.60. An analyst may describe an unbuffered area crossing; that does not satisfy this buffered rule.
Future closes, any retest, next opening price, and executable opportunity remain unknown. Preserve the map and threshold rather than lowering the buffer after observing the later outcome.

tasks.title: Process a new continuation
tasks.question: At cutoff T+1 a close of $60.80 now meets that same rule. The paper plan permits only a next opening entry at or below $60.80 and above its $58.80 stop. The next O/H/L/C is 62.00/62.50/59.00/59.50. The failure rule is a completed close below $60 within three later sessions. Write the chronological record and identify any trade P&L.
solution: Signal is recognized at T+1 close. At the next open, 62.00 exceeds the ceiling, so skip. At the later close, 59.50 is below $60 and establishes the stated chart failure. The skip has no realized trade P&L; the later low does not retroactively fill an opening-only entry.
A different later-touch order policy would be a different plan and require a feasible fill model. Save the skip and failed chart event as separate fields.

tasks.title: Diagnose a result that OHLC cannot decide
tasks.question: An alternative paper branch models 50 shares filled at $60.80. The next bar opens at $61 and has H65.20/L58.50/C61.50. Exits are stop 58.80 and target 64.80, with $5 round-trip costs and frozen $100 price-risk R. Give the two exact-level net outcomes and explain why one cannot be selected from this bar.
solution: Stop price loss = 50 × $2 = $100; net = −$105 = −1.05R. Target price profit = 50 × $4 = $200; net = +$195 = +1.95R.

The open lies between the exits and the full bar spans both. OHLC does not establish which came first. Retain sequence ambiguity or obtain suitable time-ordered data; picking the favorable path would change the evidence. Exact-level fills themselves remain teaching assumptions.
